lessons.title: Measuring resource use on site
lessons.html:
Applying resource management at work

In this work experience module you oversee the use of resources at a working abattoir under a mentor. The aim is to measure, find waste and make improvements that are safe, legal and lasting.

Set up your baseline

Before making changes, measure current performance for at least two to four weeks. Useful baseline figures include:

ResourceMeasureSource
WaterLitres per head slaughteredWater meter readings and slaughter register
ElectricitykWh per head or per tonne of carcassElectricity meter or utility bill
LabourLabour hours per head; overtime hoursTime and attendance system
YieldDressing percentage; trim kg per carcassWeighing system and trim records
By-productsHide rejects or downgrades; offal condemnedTannery feedback and inspection records
ChemicalsLitres per week; concentration checksStock issues and test strips
DowntimeMinutes per shift by causeShift reports and maintenance logs

Read the meters properly

Read meters at the same time each day and write down the reading, date and your name. Calculate the daily use by subtracting yesterday's reading from today's. Divide by the number of animals slaughtered to get use per head. Compare days with similar slaughter numbers and species.

Look for patterns

High water use on cleaning nights, high electricity on hot days, more overtime on Mondays or more trims from one supplier all point to specific causes you can investigate.

lessons.title: Running an improvement project
lessons.html:
Choose one clear target

During work experience, plan and run at least one improvement project with your mentor. Choose something measurable and within your control, for example reducing water use during cleaning, reducing bruising trims, or reducing waiting time at the start of the shift.

Plan, do, check, act

  1. Plan: state the problem with figures, find the causes, choose actions, set a target and date. Example: Water use averages 1 200 litres per head of cattle. Target: 1 050 litres within six weeks without affecting hygiene.
  2. Do: carry out the actions, such as fitting trigger nozzles, fixing three leaks found in a walk-through, and training cleaners in dry cleaning first.
  3. Check: measure again for several weeks. Check hygiene results such as swabs and pre-operational checks have not got worse.
  4. Act: if it worked, make it standard practice (update the SOP and train everyone). If not, look again at the causes.

Involve the team

Explain the project at the start-of-shift meeting. Ask workers where they see waste. Share progress on a simple chart. People support changes they helped design.

Calculate the savings

Convert results into rand where possible. For example, saving 150 litres per head on 200 cattle a day saves 30 000 litres a day. Multiply by the municipal tariff per kilolitre (check your water bill) to show the financial benefit, and add the reduced effluent charges if they apply.

Never compromise

Resource savings must never reduce hygiene, inspection, animal welfare or worker safety. If a saving idea affects any of these, discuss it with the quality manager, inspector or safety representative before trying it.

lessons.title: Reporting and sustaining the gains
lessons.html:
Writing up your project

Your project report is part of your portfolio of evidence. Keep it short and factual:

  1. Problem: what was wasted and how much (baseline figures).
  2. Causes: what you found and how.
  3. Actions: what was done, by whom and when.
  4. Results: figures before and after, with a simple chart.
  5. Effect on hygiene, safety and quality: evidence that they were not harmed.
  6. Financial benefit: estimated saving per month or year.
  7. Next steps: how the gains will be kept and what else could be improved.

Ask your mentor to sign the report and add comments.

Sustaining the gains

Many improvements fade after a few weeks when attention moves elsewhere. To keep them:

  • Update SOPs and checklists with the new method.
  • Train all shifts, including new and relief workers.
  • Keep measuring and show the figures regularly.
  • Add the measure to the supervisor's shift report.
  • Recognise teams that maintain the improvement.

Day-to-day resource habits

Alongside the project, show your mentor that you manage resources every shift: closing chiller doors, reporting leaks, balancing the line, approving overtime only when needed, controlling consumables and preventing bruising and hide damage. Record examples in your logbook.

Key points

  • Measure a baseline before making changes.
  • Use meter readings and records to calculate use per head.
  • Run an improvement project using plan, do, check, act.
  • Show savings in figures and rand, and prove hygiene and safety were not harmed.
  • Sustain gains by updating SOPs, training and continued measurement.
